bio.en: Janna Bastow is co-founder and CEO of ProdPad, the product management tool, and co-creator of Mind the Product, the global product management community and conference series.
bio.zh: Janna Bastow 是产品管理工具 ProdPad 的联合创始人兼 CEO，也是全球产品管理社区与会议系列 Mind the Product 的共同创办人。

summary.en: In this conversation, Janna shares hard-won lessons from building both a product-management software company and the world's largest product community. She covers how to run effective product strategy and roadmapping, how to engage stakeholders and keep a roadmap outcome-driven rather than feature-driven, and what years of watching thousands of PMs have taught her about what good product management looks like. The episode is a practical guide for product leaders who want to sharpen how their teams think and operate.
summary.zh: 在这期对话中，Janna 分享了她同时打造一家产品管理软件公司和全球最大产品社区的来之不易的经验。她讲了如何做有效的产品战略与路线图、如何调动干系人并让路线图以“成果”而非“功能”为导向，以及多年来观察成千上万名 PM 后她对“好产品管理”的理解。这期节目是想提升团队思考与运作方式的产品领导者的实用指南。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: The whole point about a roadmap is that it's not designed to be your plan. I think about it as being a prototype for your strategy. What I mean by that is we talk about prototyping all the time in the lean world and a prototype is essentially a way of checking your assumptions. Generally, we think about it in terms of a design or like a model, but think about it at the strategy level.
turns.zh: 路线图的核心意义在于，它并非旨在成为你的最终计划。我把它视为你战略的原型。我的意思是，在精益理念中，我们总在谈论原型，而原型本质上是验证假设的一种方式。通常，我们会从设计或模型角度去理解它，但在战略层面，我们需要更宏观的视角。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So at the feature level, you'd prototype by doing a design, a mockup, and you'd take that mockup and you'd share it with somebody and say, "Here's a mockup of the feature that I'm trying to build. What do you think?" And they'd tell you what's right or wrong, and you'd add some new copy or a button to make it more clear, and you'd throw out the original prototype, because it wasn't very good and you'd make a new one. So the value isn't the prototype, the value is in the prototyping process.
turns.zh: 所以在功能层面，你会通过设计原型、制作模型来验证想法，然后将模型分享给别人，问他们：“这是我要开发的功能模型，你们觉得怎么样？”对方会指出优缺点，你会添加新的文案或按钮来优化设计，最终淘汰旧的原型，因为它不够完善，再重新制作新版本。因此，原型的价值不在于本身，而在于原型过程。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: The value isn't in your roadmap, the value is in the roadmapping process. What you're actually doing is laying out your assumptions of the problems that you're solving. So you're saying, "I think we have this problem, then this problem. What do you think?" The whole point is that you just share your early assumptions with other people on the team, with customers, even, like anybody who will listen and just check that you're on the right path.
turns.zh: 路线图的价值不在于最终的文档，而在于制定路线图的过程。实际上，你是在列出解决问题的初步假设。比如你会说：“我认为我们面临这样一个问题，然后是另一个问题。你们怎么看？”关键在于，你要把早期假设与团队成员、客户甚至任何愿意倾听的人分享，验证方向是否正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Janna, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Janna，欢迎做客本播客。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Hi, thanks so much for having me.
turns.zh: 嗨，非常感谢邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's my pleasure. Just to start off and set a little context for folks, could you give listeners a 55 second background on what you've been up to in your career?
turns.zh: 很荣幸。首先，为听众简要介绍一下您的职业生涯背景吧？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So I'm a product manager by background. I started my career falling into product management like a lot of people do, accidentally. I worked my way up to be head of product at a startup in London. And then saw the need for product management tools, because there wasn't really anything like that out there. So started building ProdPad. One of my co-founders, who I also happened to start Mind the Product with, and Mind the Product turned into the world's largest community of product managers. So I ended up founding two things at the same time, and that's what kept me busy for the last decade or so.
turns.zh: 好的，我出身产品经理背景。职业生涯初期和许多人一样误打误撞进入了产品管理领域。在伦敦一家初创公司担任产品负责人后，发现市场缺乏专业的产品管理工具，于是创立了ProdPad。我的联合创始人也是我共同创办Mind the Product的伙伴，Mind the Product后来发展为全球最大的产品经理社区。因此，我同时创立了两家公司，这也是过去十多年来让我忙得不可开交的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And currently you have a company, maybe just mentioned that, before we move on, because I think it'll be important.
turns.zh: 目前您还有一家公司，之前提过，但可能还需要再详细说下，因为我觉得这很重要。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yep, absolutely. So that tool that I was talking about turned into ProdPad, which is software for product people. So it's a tool that allows you to build roadmaps and do your OKRs and capture ideas from your team and feedback from your customer and just organize all your product managements stuff in one space.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。我之前提到的那个工具后来发展成了ProdPad，这是一款面向产品经理的软件。它能帮助你制定路线图、完成OKR、收集团队意见和客户反馈，还能把所有产品管理工作整合到一个平台上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So you mentioned Mind the Product and ProductTank, which is kind of this associated component. I'm not exactly sure the difference, but I know they're related. One's a community component, right? Is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你之前提到了Mind the Product和ProductTank，这两个似乎是相关联的项目。我不太清楚它们的区别，但知道它们有联系。一个是社区组件，对吧？对吧？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So I think you mentioned it's probably the biggest product community in the world, both online and offline. And as someone that's building their own community around the newsletter and the podcast that I have, I'm always curious just to learn what folks have learned about building communities, especially for product people. So question on my mind is, what do you think has been most important in getting Mind the Product community right early on, and then also just maintaining the quality of the community?
turns.zh: 对。所以我觉得你提到它可能是全球最大的产品社区，无论是线上还是线下。作为一个围绕新闻通讯和播客建立自己社区的人，我一直很好奇，想了解大家在打造社区方面有哪些心得，特别是针对产品经理的社区。所以我有个问题：你认为早期让Mind the Product社区运作良好，然后保持社区质量的关键因素是什么？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Honestly, it wasn't so much that we set out to build a community, it was that we got together with some product people with the idea that we didn't know what we were doing. And so we figured if we got together with some other product people and started chatting it through, we'd all learn together. And so it was just the sense of sharing and collaborating and learning from each other and just keeping it as grassroots as possible as it grew. And consistency as well, just always being there, every month, holding a ProductTank, every year of holding an event. But just being there, whenever there was a chance to be there.
turns.zh: 说实话，我们一开始并没有刻意去打造一个社区，而是和一些产品经理聚在一起，当时我们自己也不知道该怎么做。于是我们想，如果能和其他产品经理一起交流、互相学习，大家就能共同成长。所以社区的核心理念就是分享、合作和相互学习，并且在发展过程中尽可能保持草根性质。还有保持一致性也很重要，每个月都要举办ProductTank活动，每年都要举办大型活动。但只要有机会，就要参与其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I'm hearing is just putting in the time, doing it consistently. I imagine a big part of it was having the right sort of people involved early on that are maybe the right exemplars of the type of community you want to build. Is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 所以我听说关键在于投入时间、保持一致性。我想早期吸引到合适的人也很重要，他们可能成为你想要打造的社区典范。对吧？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I mean surround yourself with the people who are going to help you continue that community and are going to help you with that consistency, and going to help you surround you with more and more of the right people. One of the things we learned really early on was that we only had so wide of a network. And so being able to get other people to help us curate and bring in other smart people to help find other speakers outside of our network, and help find people to write on the blog when we'd run out things to rant about. Similar to what you do, Lenny, you've got people from all over your community helping to contribute to the wider picture.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。就是要身边围绕着能帮助你维持社区运作、保持一致性的人，同时吸引更多合适的人加入。我们很早就意识到我们的社交网络范围有限。所以我们需要其他人帮忙筛选和引入优秀人才，比如在我们的圈子之外寻找演讲嘉宾，或者当我们没素材可吐槽时邀请博客作者写作。就像你做的，Lenny，你的社区里也有来自各地的人帮忙丰富内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What's the scale of the community at this point?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那现在社区的规模有多大？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: That's a good question. I don't have the exact number. What you might not know or what you might know is that Mind the Product was actually sold earlier this year, so I don't have-
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。我没有具体数字。不过你可能知道或者听说过，Mind the Product今年早些时候被出售了，所以我不掌握具体数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. I did know that.
turns.zh: 嗯，我确实知道这事。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: ... a handle on the exact numbers now. And it did go influx when COVID hit. I know at one point in time the ProductTank was like 200 going on almost 300 cities around the world. I don't know what that number is today. I know that it sort of went up and then down and then back up again. Some of those are digital still, some of those are back in-person. I know that there's thousands and thousands of product people around the world who are taking part in the community in one way, shape, or form or the other. And, of course, some people take part in the big conferences as well.
turns.zh: 嗯……目前我还不太清楚具体数字。新冠疫情来袭时，我们的社区确实遭遇了用户流失。我记得当时ProductTank在全球约200个城市，快要扩展到300个了。但如今具体数字如何，我不太清楚。社区规模曾起起落落，线上活动和线下活动交替开展。全球有成千上万的产品从业者以各种形式参与到这个社区中来。当然，也有很多人参加大型会议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine there were some mistakes that you made along the way building this community.
turns.zh: 我猜在打造这个社区的过程中，你们也遇到过不少挑战。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Oh God.
turns.zh: 天啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that stands out as, "Oh, man, we shouldn't have done that"? For folks that are thinking about building communities these days,
turns.zh: 有没有什么事让你后悔说：“哎呀，我们当时真不该那么做”？对于如今想打造社区的人来说，

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: When running a conference, it's one of the most expensive and unleanest things you can possibly do. It's really difficult as a product person to pull that off, because it pulls at your heart. You want to do something that's lean iterative, but you can't. If something screws up with the lunch order, for example, you can't fix it. You have to wait until the next year and you just have to pull out whatever you can to make it good enough for that particular year. There was a year once when we ordered food and it didn't turn out to be enough, because the caters under delivered, and we ended up having to get all our volunteers to go to the local sandwich shops and buy all the food up and bring it in.It was stuff like that that was difficult at the time, but we made do with what we could and we ended up sending cash cards to our attendee saying, "Here, let's make it up to you." Stuff like that, that just becomes logistically really, really difficult when you're just thinking, "Oh, we just pay a supplier and they make it happen." It's not that simple.
turns.zh: 举办会议是最昂贵、最不灵活的选择之一。作为产品经理，要想成功举办会议实在太难了，因为这会牵动你的情感。你想做精益迭代，但又无能为力。比如午餐订单出了问题，你根本无法补救，只能等到下一年再重新安排。有一年我们订的餐食不足，因为餐饮公司供货不足，最后只好让志愿者去当地三明治店购买食物补齐。当时这些问题确实棘手，但我们只能想办法解决，最后给参会者发了现金卡，说：“嘿，算我们请客。”这类事情在后勤方面会变得异常复杂，不能简单地说“找个供应商就能搞定”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. But that's a plus one for me to never run a conference, something I never want to do. And this is a reminder of all the pain that goes into them.
turns.zh: 明白了。好吧。这让我更坚定了永不举办会议的决心——这绝对不是我想做的事。同时也让我深刻意识到举办会议的种种难处。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Conferences are ridiculously hard. I mean the thing that I've learned is when something goes wrong in a conference, it doesn't happen in the hundreds of dollars of cost, it happens in the thousands of dollars of cost. A speaker who decides they can't make it for one reason or the other, totally legitimate reason, sure, but you've already paid for their business class flights, and so you've got to find another speaker last minute and get them over. That's thousands of pounds in the hole. It could be things like the printing went wrong and you found out the day before, that's more dollars gone. There's lots of things that could go wrong. Our venue once went bust, the after party venue once went bust three weeks before the conference. That was year one.
turns.zh: 举办会议实在太难了。我学到的教训是，一旦会议出问题，就不是几百美元的损失，而是几千美元的损失。某位演讲者临时退出（当然，合理原因除外），但你已经为他们的商务舱机票付了钱，只能紧急找替补演讲者飞过来。那就是几千英镑的损失。印刷材料出错、后续派对场地倒闭之类的问题都可能发生。第一年，我们的场地在会议前三周倒闭了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: All of these things, yeah, that's what we said, "Super, what are we supposed to do?" We ended up having to just make do and found somewhere else and roll with it. So lots of things that go wrong at that sort of level. But the thing is that we built up a lot of goodwill with the community and were able to get help from people around us, get suggestions from people around us. And when things ended up, actually it turns out we ended up with a smaller venue than we expected, or this was slightly different or whatever else, we had people forgive us. It worked out okay, in our favor.
turns.zh: 所有这些事情，是啊，我们当时就是这么说的，"太棒了，我们该怎么办呢？"结果我们只能随机应变，另找场地继续推进。在这种级别的活动中，总会有各种突发状况。但关键是，我们与社区建立了良好的关系，得到了周围人的帮助和建议。当最终结果不如预期——比如场地规模缩小、活动形式有所调整之类——人们还是会体谅我们。最终结果还算不错，对我们有利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just while on this topic, I'm most curious, are conferences like a good business? Do they make a ton of money in some occasions? Is it always just super thin margin? How does that even business work?
turns.zh: 说到这个话题，我最感兴趣的是，会议行业真的能盈利吗？有些时候他们能赚大钱吗？利润率通常很低吗？这种业务模式到底是如何运作的？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: It's not for the faint hearted. It's hugely risky. In hindsight, I'm highly surprised we actually made it through some of those first ones. If you can do it, there are some amazing ways that you can monetize them. But it only starts making a difference at larger figures, and it takes a lot of efforts to actually get to that point. Somebody once asked me like, "Oh, we're struggling to sell tickets. How do you sell all those tickets?" We'll start a community several years before and invite people and run a thing, some sort of community meetup every month time, time again beforehand, and that's your marketing.
turns.zh: 这可不是胆小者能做的。风险极高。回过头来看，我很惊讶我们居然能挺过最初的几次尝试。如果你能做好这件事，就有无数变现的机会。但只有达到一定规模才能真正实现盈利，而要达到这个规模需要付出巨大努力。曾有人问我："哦，我们卖票卖得很困难，你们是怎么卖出那么多票的？"我们早在几年前就开始组建社区，定期举办各类活动，每个月都重复同样的流程，这就是我们的营销方式。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Just if you undersell tickets to a conference, for example, it can absolutely break it. And you see sometimes conferences, they run one and they don't have enough people turning up and it's gone. That can just break it. It's ridiculous. Something like COVID comes by and it can break it. It's a ridiculously hard business. It's really hard to ensure against. It's really hard to think of all the things that could go wrong and protect against. So while there are some upsides, it's not for the faint hearted.
turns.zh: 比如，如果会议门票卖得不好，整个活动就可能崩盘。有时会议举办后，参与人数不足，直接宣告失败。这简直太糟糕了。新冠疫情来袭，也可能让整个活动泡汤。这真是极其艰难的行业。要规避风险，防范各种可能出错的情况，实在太难了。所以虽然也有好处，但胆小者还是别尝试了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. That's another plus one. I have a friend who runs events here in San Francisco and I'm always just like, "How can someone be excited about running events over and over? It's so stressful and full of risk and there's always things going wrong. You can't ever have fun at these things." So it's always a different personality.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。这又多了一个赞同我的理由。我有个朋友在旧金山组织活动，我总是问他："怎么会有人热衷于反复组织活动呢？压力太大，风险太高，总有各种状况。根本没法从中获得乐趣。"可见这需要截然不同的心态。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah, event organizer or event manager or something like that was once listed as one of the most stressful jobs out there. And you can see why. It's because it all just lands on you all at once. And once the event is over, there's the sense of [foreign language 00:12:29], as in it's over and now what? The next day you're just like, "Yay." You can look at the tweet stream of everything that happened. You can look back at the photos and then you're like, "What do we do next?"
turns.zh: 是啊，活动组织者或活动经理之类的职位曾被列为压力最大的工作之一。原因很明显，所有压力一下子都压在你身上。活动结束后，那种如释重负的感觉——活动结束了，接下来该做什么？第二天你又会兴奋地说："耶！"回看活动推特动态，翻看照片，然后又问："接下来做什么？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Start prepping for ext year.
turns.zh: 开始为明年做准备。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: You start prepping for next year, off we go again. And it's really hard work. But there again, product management was also listed as one of the toughest jobs, one of the hardest jobs out there. I'm not sure if that still stands, but I know product management as it stood 10 years ago, five, 10 years ago, certainly did have a different vibe to it, and it was a really tough job.
turns.zh: 为明年做准备，然后再出发。这确实是个艰巨的任务。不过话说回来，产品管理也曾被列为最具挑战性的工作之一。我不确定现在是否还是如此，但就10年前、5年前、10年前的产品管理而言，确实有着截然不同的氛围，那确实是个高压职位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Continues to be a very tough job. On the topic of conferences and speaking, I've watched a bunch of your talks online before we started chatting today. And a couple things I noticed. One is you're just an awesome speaker, and you're also storyteller. And something that comes up a lot on this podcast is just how important communication skills are to product leaders and product managers and storytelling. And you've also seen a bunch of people do awesome talks at these conferences. So I'm just curious, whatever you have in mind, what has helped you become a better speaker and storyteller? And then also what have you seen is important to folks that are really good at storytelling and presenting at a conference, let's say?
turns.zh: 这仍然是一项极具挑战性的工作。关于会议和演讲主题，在我们今天开始聊天之前，我在网上观看了你的一些演讲。其中有几点让我印象深刻。首先，你是一位非常出色的演讲者，同时也是一位讲故事的高手。这个播客中经常提到的主题是，沟通技巧对产品负责人、产品经理以及讲故事能力的重要性。而你也见证了许多人在这些会议上进行精彩的演讲。所以我很好奇，无论你有什么想法，是什么帮助你成为更出色的演讲者和讲故事高手？另外，你认为对那些在会议上善于讲故事和展示的人来说，哪些方面是至关重要的？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Right. Yeah, such a good question. I mean, I have learned by watching a lot of other people. One of the things that I have been super lucky in my career is that by being part of Mind the Product I've gotten to watch every last Mind the Product speaker, top end speakers. I've been able to see every ProductTank London speaker, and a lot of the other ProductTank speakers around the world. Been able to see what people react to, what works, what doesn't work. So I've been able to develop a taste for a good talk and a good presentation and that sort of thing.
turns.zh: 好的。嗯，这确实是个好问题。我是说，通过观察其他人，我学到了很多东西。在我的职业生涯中，我非常幸运的一点是，通过参与Mind the Product社区，我得以观看每一位Mind the Product演讲者的演讲，尤其是顶级演讲者。我还观看过伦敦ProductTank的所有演讲者，以及全球其他ProductTank活动的许多演讲者。我能够了解到哪些内容能引起听众共鸣，哪些方法行之有效，哪些则不然。因此，我逐渐培养了对精彩演讲和出色展示的鉴赏力。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: But also one of the things that Mind the Product has been able to provide to speakers is a speaker coach. So when I was invited to speak on the Mind the Product stage in 2017, one of the things that they provided to me was an actual speaker coach, somebody to take my talk and improve on it. And it was really nerve-wracking taking my half-written talk, which I started months and months before, it started off with just Post-It Notes scattered along the wall, which I tried to turn into something. And I think it was probably six hours worth of content. And I brought this to this speaker coach, and I had a vague script idea of what I wanted to say.
turns.zh: 此外，Mind the Product为演讲者提供的服务之一是演讲指导教练。例如，2017年我受邀在Mind the Product舞台上演讲时，他们为我配备了一位演讲指导教练，帮助我改进演讲内容。当时，我准备的演讲稿写了好几个月，起初只是贴满墙壁的便利贴，后来逐渐成形。但内容可能长达六个小时。我把这份演讲稿交给指导教练时，自己对演讲内容的构思还很模糊。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And she said to me, one of the first things, she said, "Well, I've taken your script and I've turned it around. I've rewritten the jokes to land a little bit better." I was like, "That's great. I had jokes." And she helped turn the stories around, so that they carried through. She helped with posture. She helped with delivery. She helped with even just phrasing of words. Just making sure that everything landed in particular ways. And one of the things she did was make me listen to it and play it back, which I had not done before. And I still hate doing to this day, but am now more used to it than before.And I don't think anybody likes listening to the sound of their own voice. I don't think anybody likes doing that. But it does help with it. If you've got a large presentation, a big presentation, you've got to get up to that level. If you're nervous about doing it in front of a 1,000 people, then getting to that level that you're actually willing to, able to hear yourself do it, and you're able to do the talk flawlessly in the shower, and as you're walking to work, and as you're doing your groceries and all that sort of stuff, then it makes a big difference.
turns.zh: 她首先对我说：“我改了你的剧本，让笑话更自然。”我回答：“太棒了。我确实有笑话。”她还帮助我调整了故事结构，使其更连贯。她指导了我的姿势、表达方式，甚至是用词选择。确保每个环节都恰到好处。她还让我反复试听自己的演讲，这在当时对我来说很陌生。直到现在我还是不太喜欢这样做，但已经比以前习惯多了。毕竟没人喜欢听自己说话的声音，也没人乐意这么做，但这确实很有帮助。如果你要做一场大型演讲，就必须达到那个水准。如果你对在1000人面前演讲感到紧张，那么先在小范围内练习，确保自己能流畅完成演讲——无论是在淋浴时、走路去上班时，还是在超市排队时，都能完美演绎——这会带来巨大的改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one tactic that I love that you shared is record yourself, watch yourself ,keep refining, but watching your actual performance. Looking back at the lessons your coach taught you for new presentations that you do, is there anything else that sticks with you? Or just let's make sure to get X, Y, Z nailed because that'll help make this talk better.
turns.zh: 嗯，你提到的其中一个方法是先录制自己演讲的视频，观看录像并不断改进。这里有个关键点——关注你的实际表现。回顾教练教给你的新演讲技巧时，有没有什么特别印象深刻的部分？或者说，我们只要确保 X、Y、Z 这些关键点做好了，就能让整个演讲更出色。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: One of the things that I've stopped doing is I used to sit down with a PowerPoint and start writing my deck in PowerPoint or Slides, now. What I now do is I start with my story points. I start with my narratives. I try to figure out what I'm actually trying to say, and then I fit it into the deck. Because what I was doing before, I would get stuck in this mode of the presentation mode, and trying to make the presentation, the slides fit my narrative as opposed to the opposite way around. Having a great narrative, and the slides should follow more naturally.
turns.zh: 我现在改掉了以前的习惯。以前我会先坐下来用 PowerPoint 制作幻灯片，但现在我会先构思故事主线和叙事框架。先想清楚自己真正想传达的信息，再根据内容来设计幻灯片。以前我总陷入演讲模式的怪圈，试图让幻灯片去适应叙事结构，而不是反过来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about just the presenting, the physical anxiety of presenting?, Is there anything you've done there to get better with that and feel-
turns.zh: 关于演讲时的紧张感呢？有没有什么应对方法能帮助你克服心理障碍，让你更自在？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Oh, yes.
turns.zh: 哦，有的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... more comfortable?
turns.zh: …更放松？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So one of the things that actually really does work is the power pose, standing with your hands on your hips and it really does, I'm not sure if it's adrenaline or endorphins or something, it releases some sort of chemicals that really does just help boost your confidence and make you feel better as you're getting ready to stand on stage. And it something that's me and other Mind the Product speakers, and I've done behind all the big stages that I've done in recent years. Stand there with your hands on your hips and just feel better about it as opposed to sitting there balling up in that tense pile of stress.
turns.zh: 其实有个很有效的技巧叫“力量姿势”——双手叉腰站立。不知道是肾上腺素还是内啡肽的作用，这种姿势能释放某种化学物质，增强自信，让你更有状态。最近几年我在大舞台上演讲前都会这么做，效果很明显。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: One of the other things that I always do, if I get a chance to, is get out onto the stage sooner rather later. So when they do the tech check, just walk out onto the stage and just wonder back and forth and look out to the audience and greet it. There's no one there. It's the day before, it's completely empty. But look up at the audience and just enjoy that sweep of the audience, and just get used to it. And imagine it full of people. Don't imagine them naked, that doesn't matter. But just imagine them there, so that when you actually do see them the next day, it's not so stressful.
turns.zh: 还有一点很重要，如果有机会的话，我总会尽早熟悉舞台环境。比如在技术调试阶段，就走上舞台来回走动，观察观众，跟他们互动。当时台下没人，前一天的演讲完全空场，但你可以想象观众满场的样子，甚至可以想象他们没穿衣服（当然这没关系），反正要把他们当成真实存在的人，这样第二天正式演讲时就不会那么紧张了。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: One of the other things I try to do is find the people in the audience who are your fans. And you'll find them in the course of your talk. There's always going to be some people in the audience who just look bored and they're on your phone, just ignore them. They're always going to be there. Find the people who are nodding along and smiling and going, "Yeah, yeah, that's me. That's me." And just speak to them. And if you find one up there and one over there and one down there, no one's going to notice that you're doing your talk just to them. And just keep delivering your talk around the room to these few key people. They're having a great time, you're having a great time, and you're doing a great talk as a result.
turns.zh: 另外，我还会寻找台下的“粉丝”。演讲过程中总能发现一些专注听讲、频频点头的人。要多和他们互动。哪怕台上台下各有一个，旁人也不会察觉你只对他们讲话。这样就能把演讲重点锁定在这些核心听众身上。他们乐在其中，演讲效果也会自然提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such good advice. The power pose piece, you said that it's hands on hips. I think there's also when we raise your hands up and you're like Superman or something. I think there's-
turns.zh: 这真是个好建议。关于摆出权威姿势那部分，你说要把手放在臀部。我觉得还有那种把手举向天空，摆出超人姿势的动作。还有——

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: That could work, yeah.
turns.zh: 这招应该挺管用的，是吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think people have different ones. Also, I've seen that, there's like all the science that showed that was effective and then I think it was one of those experiments that wasn't replicatable. People are kind of worried that there's not real science backing that up. But I've done that myself and it actually works. And so it doesn't matter ,if it works for you, just do it.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得不同的人有不同的方法。我还见过一些科学研究证明这种方法有效，但后来发现那些实验结果不可重复。人们担心缺乏科学依据。不过我自己试过，还真有效。所以只要对你有用，就大胆去做。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah. If it's a placebo, hey, don't tell me that, it works. Honestly, I feel better at the end of it, and get on stage and do a better job.
turns.zh: 是啊。如果这是安慰剂效应，管他呢，效果好就行。说实话，我每次讲完都感觉状态更好地上台，表现得也更出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Someone made this point, placebo is this magical thing that we have in our brains that gets things to change by not having anything go. You just change things. It's amazing. It's magical.
turns.zh: 有人提到过，安慰剂是我们大脑里的神奇机制，即使没有实际药物也能产生效果。真是不可思议。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah. Placebos are as effective as the actual drug, whatever. I'm happy with a placebo. Just don't break the placebo effect for me. That would be fine, right?
turns.zh: 对啊。有时候安慰剂和真正的药物效果一样。我就乐意接受安慰剂效应，只要别打破它就行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That's right. One last question on the speaking stuff. How bad were you initially? Just because folks probably see you, see some of your talks and they're like, "Oh, my god, I'm never going to be this good. I'm screwed."
turns.zh: 没错。最后一个关于演讲的问题。你最初有多糟糕？可能很多人看了你的演讲后会想：“天啊，我永远也达不到这种水平，我完了。”

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah, I used to be shaky, little fawn, shaky voice, terrified at the front. Okay. So it was one of the first ever ProductCamp events that we were running. And the first one I think I did okay at, but it was a smaller group, it who's only like 50 or so people. And the second one it had ballooned to 200 people. This is more product people than I'd ever known. And they were all super professional, and they're all looking at me. And I stood at the front of this group and I was supposed to just, I don't know, tell them what they were supposed to be doing that day. And I had it all half written down, and I started talking and then I sort just tripped up over what I was saying and forgot everything and blanked. And I just looked up and I went, "I'm really sorry everybody. I'm just going to start again."
turns.zh: 是啊，我以前很紧张，声音颤抖，在台上很胆怯。好吧，那是我们举办的首批ProductCamp活动之一。我觉得自己第一场表现还不错，但那只是小型活动，观众只有50人左右。第二场观众激增到200人。这里汇聚了比我见过的更多产品从业者，他们都非常专业，眼睛都盯着我。我站在台前本该告诉他们当天的日程安排，但准备的稿子只写了一半，刚开口就卡壳，全忘词了。最后我抬头说了句：“大家对不起，我重新开始吧。”

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And I started again. I said, "Hi everybody, I'm Janna and welcome to ProductCamp." And I just started again and they were just totally fine with it. Honestly, it was fine. And this is the thing that I've learned since then is people in the audience are rooting for you. They were totally cool with this. They didn't think anything of it and they just rolled with it, as did I. And so whenever I see somebody who's struggling on stage, just give them a nod, a smile, clap them along, give them reassuring looks, and hopefully they'll just pull through.
turns.zh: 重新开始。我说：“大家好，我是Janna，欢迎参加ProductCamp。”然后继续讲，他们完全没意见。说实话，这没什么大不了的。从那以后我明白，听众其实都在支持你。他们不在意你的失误，顺其自然，我也是如此。所以当你看到台上有人遇到困难时，只要点头微笑、鼓掌、给予鼓励的眼神，他们就能振作起来。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And if you ever feel like you're shaking, you're corpsing on stage, you're falling apart, honestly, just take a deep breath and just pick up where you last remembered you were and just keep going. Honestly, no one is rooting for you to fall over and have a bad time. Everyone's rooting for you to finish your point and get on with it.
turns.zh: 如果觉得自己发抖、在台上崩溃、乱了节奏，深呼吸，回到你记得的最后一个环节，继续下去。说真的，没人希望你出丑，每个人都希望你顺利完成演讲，继续下一个环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a great story and it's a good example of people have this fear of the worst case scenario. Everything's going to fall apart. They're going to be seen as idiots, they don't know what they're doing. It's all going to be revealed on stage, because you screw up in how you're talking. And the worst case scenario never happens, in my experience. And two,, if it does, just do exactly what you said, just try to start again. It's easy to say, hard to do. This isn't a conscious thing that people can get over. It's like your body's just doing crazy shit and you're so nervous sometimes and can't just rationalize it to like, "Nah, it'll be fine." But, yeah, it's fine. To your point, people want you to be awesome and succeed. They're not there to like, "Ha, ha, you stopped. You screwed up."
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的故事，也是人们害怕最坏情况发生的一个典型例子。一切都会崩盘。他们会被视为白痴，不知道自己在做什么。这一切都会在舞台上暴露出来，因为你说话时会出错。而在我的经验中，最坏的情况从未发生过。另外，就算真的发生了，只要按照你之前说好的去做，重新开始就行。这说起来容易，做起来难。这不是人们能克服的有意识行为。这就像你的身体会做出疯狂的举动，有时你会非常紧张，无法理性地想"没事的，会好起来的"。但其实真的没事。你说得对，人们希望你表现出色，取得成功。他们不会幸灾乐祸地说，"哈，你停下来了。你搞砸了。"

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And it's humanizing when you screw up, right? People don't like people who are perfectly perfect and don't mess up, and it makes them feel like they can't go up and go do their talk. I mean I think that right there showed everybody else that they could go up on the little ProductCamp stages that day and go do their own talks. And they certainly wouldn't be any worse than that. As long as I just remembered their name, they'd be fine. Crack on, they got it.
turns.zh: 而当你出错时，反而更能拉近人与人之间的距离，对吧？人们不喜欢完美无缺、从不犯错的人，这会让他们觉得自己无法上台演讲。我觉得那次演讲向其他人展示了，他们当天也可以登上ProductCamp的舞台，进行自己的演讲。只要我能记住他们的名字，他们就能成功。加油，他们能行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of screwing up, you have some very spicy takes on roadmap and roadmaps.
turns.zh: 说到出错，你对路线图和路线图规划有一些非常尖锐的看法。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Ooh, yes, I do.
turns.zh: 哦，是的，我确实有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then generally the mistakes people make in organizing the roadmap. So I definitely want to spend some time here. So first of all, you have some strong feelings against Gantt based road mapping. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 然后一般来说，人们在组织路线图时会犯的错误。所以我肯定想在这方面多花点时间。首先，你对基于甘特图的路线图规划有强烈的反感。你能谈谈这个吗？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah, sure. I used to do timeline roadmapping. The first version of ProdPad was actually a timeline roadmap. So to take you back, when I was a junior product manager, mid-level product manager, I used to do my roadmap like everyone else was doing the road, as in I looked up what a roadmap was, and it looked like a colorful Gantt chart. I knew what a Gantt chart was. And so I started putting one together, which is where I'd take the features that I was working on and line them up against their due dates. And I would get a little pat on the head from my boss, and they'd say, "Good job, now go deliver it," basically.
turns.zh: 嗯，当然。我以前做过时间线路线图。ProdPad的第一个版本实际上就是一个时间线路线图。所以回想一下，我还是初级产品经理、中级产品经理的时候，做路线图和其他人一样，就是查阅路线图是什么样子的，看起来像一个彩色甘特图。我知道甘特图是什么。所以我就开始整理一个，把我正在开发的功能和它们的截止日期对应起来。我会得到老板的一点表扬，他们会说，"干得好，现在去交付吧。"基本上就是这样。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And I would do my best with delivery, and I'd never quite be able to deliver everything. Something would always get in the way. But I sort of assumed that was my fault. I just wasn't great at delivery, and I just had to get a little bit better at adding enough buffer and setting expectations and doing a roadmap slightly better. But I figured that this is how everyone was doing the roadmaps, and it was just me who wasn't finishing the stuff on the roadmap quite right.
turns.zh: 然后我会尽力交付，但总是不太能完成所有任务。总会有事情插进来。但我当时以为是自己的错。我只是不擅长交付，我只需要稍微提高一点，增加一些缓冲时间，设定更合理的预期，把路线图做得更好一点。但我以为每个人都是这么做路线图的，只有我没能正确完成路线图上的任务。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And when it came to creating the first tools for roadmap, I'd envision something that would actually help me manage this format of a roadmap more easily. Which I ended up creating the very early version of ProdPad, which was a digitized version of this, where you could drag and drop ideas onto the roadmap and stretch and squeeze them, and pan the roadmap back and forth. And I shared this with some early product people that I knew, some early users, and they gave me some feedback and some of them absolutely loved it.
turns.zh: 当开始为路线图创建第一个工具时，我设想了一个能更轻松管理这种路线图格式的工具。于是我创建了ProdPad的早期版本，这是一个数字化版本，你可以在路线图上拖放想法，拉伸和压缩它们，还能来回移动路线图。我把这个分享给了一些我认识的早期产品人员和用户，他们给了我一些反馈，其中一些人非常喜欢它。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: They're like, "Yeah, this is great. Now I can stop using PowerPoints or whatever tool I'm using or drawing it up in whatever I can now start using this digitized tool." But one of the things that we started hearing from early customers is about a month later they said, "Great, but I want to take this, and move all these things here over by a month in the field." We're like, "Oh, that's interesting. We've heard that from a bunch of other people too. Now why is that?" Because had we just asked our customers, had we just built what our customers wanted, we would've just ended up with a multi-select drag and drop. But this was all built in jQuery and it was a little bit difficult to build that.
turns.zh: 他们会说：“是啊，这太棒了。现在我可以不用再用PowerPoint或其他工具来制作演示文稿了，可以直接使用这个数字化工具了。” 但大约一个月后，我们开始收到早期客户的反馈，他们说：“不错，但我想把这些内容提前一个月到现场使用。” 我们回应道：“哦，这很有意思。我们也从其他许多客户那里听到了类似的需求。那么这是为什么呢？” 因为如果我们只是按照客户的需求来开发产品，最终只会开发出一个多选拖放功能。但这个功能是用jQuery开发的，实现起来相当困难。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So we sort of asked the five whys, we dug in to why people wanted this thing, and we found out that no one was actually delivering the roadmap in the timeframe that they were saying they were. So we're like, "Wait, if it's not just us who's not living the roadmap and none of these better than us roadmap product managers are building the roadmap on time, what's the point of a roadmap? Why are we giving them a roadmap?" So that's when we sat down, it was myself and Simon, my co-founder at ProdPad, and we sat down and we came up with a three column roadmap, current, near term, future, which became now, next, later.
turns.zh: 于是我们开始追问五个为什么，深入探究客户需求背后的原因，发现根本问题在于客户无法按时交付路线图。于是我们反问：“等等，如果不只是我们无法按时交付路线图，而且其他优秀的产品经理也无法按时完成路线图，那路线图还有什么意义？为什么要给他们提供路线图？” 于是我和ProdPad的联合创始人西蒙坐下来，设计了一个三栏式路线图：当前任务、近期任务、未来任务，最终演化为即时任务、近期任务、后续任务。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And it took away the simple concept of a timeline at the top. Now, the problem with the timeline is that as soon as you have a timeline, it turns it into a math chart sort of thing, where you've got time on the X axis and things to do on the Y axis and you basically end up with everything underneath is assigned a due date or a iteration. And it seems that everything that you do has a due date, an iteration just by the format of the roadmap, which is painful. It's just wrong, because we don't have that. The further out you plan, the more you're making it up. We know this.
turns.zh: 这种设计摒弃了顶部时间线这一简单概念。时间线的问题在于，一旦引入时间线，它就变成了一个数学图表，X轴是时间，Y轴是待办事项，每个元素都被分配了截止日期或迭代周期。似乎所有任务都必须有截止日期或迭代周期，这实在令人头疼。这根本就是错误的做法，因为现实并非如此。越是长远的规划，越是靠想象填补。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And so we wanted more flexibility and we knew that other product managers wanted that flexibility, because we kept asking what they were up to. So we decided to break it down into these three buckets, and provided that as an option and people loved it. It became this first bump in our usage of ProdPad, because people went, "Oh, wait, I can just say what's happening now, what's happening next, and what's happening later? And if I want to, I can add a date to the specific thing, but I don't have to. And I can be less and less granular about that as I go forwards. Yeah."
turns.zh: 因此我们需要更大的灵活性，也知道其他产品经理也渴望这种灵活性，因为我们不断询问他们的进展。于是我们决定将其拆分为三个部分，并提供这种选项，用户反响热烈。这成为ProdPad用户使用习惯的第一个突破口，因为用户发现：“哦，等等，我可以直接说出当前正在进行的事情、接下来要做的事情、后续要做的事情。如果我愿意，还可以给具体任务添加日期，但并非必须如此。随着时间推移，我可以逐渐降低粒度要求。太棒了。”

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So it's taking from the concept of the cone of uncertainty, taking from the idea that things get less certain as they get further away, which is kind of how reality works. So the whole beef with the timeline roadmap is just taking apart the concept of the timeline. It doesn't mean we live in la la land. It doesn't mean that we don't believe in having dates on the roadmap, if there is a date that we have to work towards. It just means not penalizing ourselves by having a date on everything on the roadmap.
turns.zh: 这种设计借鉴了不确定性锥的概念，即越是长远的事情越不确定，这正是现实的运行方式。因此，批评时间线路线图的核心在于拆解时间线概念。这并不意味着我们生活在幻想世界里，也不意味着我们否认路线图上必须有截止日期，但关键在于不必为路线图上的每个任务都强制添加截止日期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. I didn't know that you could put dates on some of the things that's interesting, because I was trying to understand exactly how this approach works. We should also mentioned, you came up with this whole idea of now, next, later, which a lot of people use now. Is that right?
turns.zh: 明白了。好的，我之前不知道还能给某些任务添加日期，这挺有趣的，因为我一直想深入理解这种方法的运作原理。我们还需要提一下，你们提出的即时任务、近期任务、后续任务的分类理念，现在很多人都在使用，对吧？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So as someone that's been using Gantt timelines his whole career, I'm really curious to dig into these ideas and challenge the default assumption.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。作为一个职业生涯中一直使用甘特图的时间线的人，我真的很想深入探讨这些想法，并挑战默认假设。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to chat with my friend John Cutler from podcast sponsor Amplitude. Hey, John.
turns.zh: 我很兴奋能和我的朋友约翰·卡特勒（John Cutler）聊聊，他来自我们的播客赞助商Amplitude。嘿，约翰。

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Hey, Lenny. Excited to be here.
turns.zh: 嘿，莱尼。很高兴能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: John, give us a behind the scenes at Amplitude. When most people think of Amplitude, they think of product analytics, but now you're getting into experimentation, and even just launched a CDP. What's the thought process there?
turns.zh: 约翰，跟我们讲讲Amplitude的幕后故事吧。当大多数人想到Amplitude时，他们会想到产品分析，但现在你们正涉足实验，甚至刚刚推出了CDP。背后的思考逻辑是什么？

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Well, we've always thought of Amplitude as being about supporting the full product loop, think collect data, inform bets, ship experiments, and learn. That's the heart of growth to us. So the big aha was seeing how many customers were using Amplitude to analyze experiments, use segments for outreach, and send data to other destinations. Experiment in CDP came out of listening to and observing our customers.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们一直认为Amplitude的核心是支持完整的产品循环，包括收集数据、为决策提供依据、开展实验并从中学习。这对我们来说是增长的核心所在。最大的启发在于，我们发现许多客户正在使用Amplitude分析实验、使用细分数据进行外联，并将数据发送到其他目的地。CDP中的实验功能源于我们倾听并观察客户需求的过程中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And supporting growth and learning has always been Amplitude's core focus, right?
turns.zh: 支持增长和学习一直是Amplitude的核心重点，对吧？

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Yeah. So Amplitude tries to meet customers where they are. We just launched starter templates, and have a great scholarship program for startups. There's never been a more important time for growing.
turns.zh: 是的。所以Amplitude试图满足客户的实际需求。我们刚刚推出了入门模板，还有针对初创企业的优秀奖学金项目。当前是推动增长最重要的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely agree. Thanks for joining us, John. And head to amplitude.com to get started.
turns.zh: 完全同意。感谢约翰的加入。请访问amplitude.com开始使用吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's two questions that this brings up, and you may have answered them in part. One is just without dates on things, how do you make sure marketing and sales and your CEO has things that they need for promising or at least giving a sense of when a product will come out? And the other is just aligning internally with engineers, design being done on a certain date, engineers being done on a certain date, PMs being done a certain day, [inaudible 00:28:32]. How do you deal with those in this format?
turns.zh: 这引发了两个问题，你可能已经部分回答了其中一个。第一个是，在没有具体日期的情况下，如何确保营销、销售和CEO能够获得所需信息，以便承诺或至少让人们了解产品何时上市？另一个是如何在内部与工程师、设计师协调，确保他们在特定日期完成任务，产品经理在特定日期完成工作[00:28:32的音频缺失]。在这种模式下，你是如何应对这些问题的？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: There's a couple ways that you can turn that around. So one is you should still be having regular communication, so they can still see what's coming up in the now call them. So they have a sense of what the order of things are and that things that are in the now column are probably weeks away, not months and months away. You should probably have launch readiness meetings so people understand this is the stuff that's going through testing, and that's likely to be coming out now.
turns.zh: 有几种方法可以扭转这种局面。其一，仍需保持定期沟通，让他们能清楚了解当前任务的进展。例如，仍在“当前”列中的任务可能还需要几周而非数月才能完成。因此，应该召开发布准备会议，让大家明白这些正在测试中的功能很可能即将上线。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: But one of the other things that you can be doing for your marketing and sales teams is separating your hard launch from your soft launch. So what you should be doing is basically saying your developers are able to launch something on a particular date and it's the date that's convenient for them, right? Let's say they think that they can get something out for end of September. Now, that might be pushed to made October because things go wrong.
turns.zh: 但你可以为营销和销售团队做的一件事是将正式发布和软发布区分开。基本思路是，开发人员可以在特定日期发布产品，而这个日期对他们来说是方便的，对吧？比如说，他们认为产品能在9月底推出，但由于各种原因可能会推迟到10月。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Now at that point, whether it's end of September or mid-October, it doesn't really matter to the marketers because they're busy talking about the stuff that was launched in August. They've got lots of stuff to work on. They're selling and marketing the stuff that's already live and out there. When this new thing comes out, that's a soft launch. As soon as that soft launch is out, great, let's kick off this launch meeting with launch steps. Now you've got something else to go do. And it's so much better for marketing anyways because they're not setting up their launch steps based on something that they don't have eyes on. There's nothing worse than the marketers trying to market something based on pictures from the designers that have vastly changed by the time they go out or that they don't know whether it's going to come out on the right day or not.
turns.zh: 现阶段，无论是9月底还是10月中旬，对营销人员来说都无关紧要，因为他们正忙着推广8月推出的产品。他们有大量工作要做，销售和营销已上线并推向市场的现有产品。当新产品推出时，那只是个小范围测试。一旦测试结束，立刻召开发布会议，制定发布计划。随后他们又要投入新工作。对营销团队而言，这样做要好得多，因为他们不必基于尚未成形的信息制定发布策略。最糟糕的情况莫过于营销人员根据设计师提供的图片进行推广，而当产品实际发布时，图片已大变样，或者根本无法按时上线。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So they've actually got a functional working version that they can share with some customers. They can start getting videos of it working. They can get testimonials from early beta users. And then they can spend, whether it's two days or six days or six weeks or six months planning the biggest, bangest launch they want. They can then spend the next however long they want to launch their hard launch, and then that goes out. And in that period that they're doing that hard launch development is cracking on with their next thing.
turns.zh: 实际上，他们已有可用的功能版本，可以与部分客户分享。他们能获取产品运行的视频，收集早期测试用户的反馈。之后，他们可以用两天、六天、六周或六个月的时间筹备大型轰动性发布。然后再进行正式发布。在开发硬件发布的这段时间里，他们又能全力投入下一个项目。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And by the time that they're done that marketing is then, "Okay, great, what have you built? We're ready to work on the next thing." So you're just separating soft launch from hard launch, so that you don't have this stress of trying to line up to completely different types of projects, your marketing projects and your development projects, which is where a lot of those things fall apart.
turns.zh: 等这些工作完成后，营销团队会问：“好的，你们做了什么？我们准备好着手下一个项目了。”这样就将软性测试和硬件发布分开了，避免营销团队和开发团队因截然不同的项目周期而产生压力——这正是许多项目失败的主要原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So kind of the basic premise is roadmaps or timelines sound great and awesome. Everyone would love to know when things are going to be done and if it worked it'd be great. Oftentimes, they're all made up, they don't work, you don't hit deadlines, they're always missed. So instead of promising dates for everything you're doing, you're better off generally just giving a sense of, "Here's what we're going to work on now. Here's what's coming up next." And then for the things that really need a date, we're going to put dates on those things and give it our best shot. Is that [inaudible 00:31:29]-
turns.zh: 明白了。基本原则是，路线图或时间表听起来很棒，令人赞赏。每个人都希望知道事情何时完成，如果能成功实施就更好了。但很多时候，这些计划都是虚构的，无法实现，总是错过截止日期。因此，与其为所有正在进行的工作设定具体日期，不如大致说明：“现在我们要着手这项工作，接下来还有什么计划。”而对于确实需要日期的项目，我们会设定日期并全力以赴。是这样吗[听不清00:31:29]-

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah. That's absolutely right. If something does have to have a date, we don't live in la la land, if something has a regulatory date, when GDPR came down, everyone had a due date on the roadmap, because if you didn't hit that date then you were going to be in trouble. Sometimes you might have dates that are tied to things like the Christmas rush, or if you're in education it might be like has to be out by the school year.
turns.zh: 是的。完全正确。如果确实有必须设定日期的项目，我们可不会异想天开。例如，GDPR生效时，每个项目路线图上都标注了截止日期，因为若未能达标就会陷入麻烦。有时截止日期与圣诞节促销相关，或者教育领域的项目可能需要在学年结束前发布。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: At which point, in order to reach something by that date you have to put in more project planning work, as in you have to plan out ahead of time, you have to put in more buffer time to do that. And generally you have to plan to get that thing done well before, so that you can have a soft launch before and make sure it works and do some iteration and fix it before the actual full-on launch happens. Because if you leave it too late, it's going to go wrong and you're going to miss the deadline.
turns.zh: 到了这个时候，要想在既定日期前完成某项任务，你就必须投入更多项目规划工作，比如提前规划好整个流程，预留足够的缓冲时间来完成这些工作。通常你还需要提前很久就开始筹备，这样才能在正式上线前进行试运行，确保产品运行正常，并进行迭代和修复工作。因为如果拖到最后一刻才行动，往往会出问题，最终导致错过截止日期。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: If you did that for all of your launches, you're just going to end up either cutting quality, because everything's just going to be big crap cause it's going to be pushing it out the door last minute. Or you're just going to end up spending so much time trying to plan things to the nth degree that you're just going to move super slow. This is why you end up with teams who are really big but can't deliver worth anything. Where compared to these tiny teams, who are just out delivering them and just spinning things out the door, they're the ones who aren't spending all their time going, "Are we certain this is going to deliver? And how many hours is this going to take you? And let me go talk to this person, find out how many days it's going to take him," and back and forth and back and forth. They're just building, and it goes faster.
turns.zh: 如果你对所有项目都采取这种做法，最终要么只能降低质量标准，因为产品会被仓促推出；要么就会陷入过度规划的死循环，进展极其缓慢。这就是为什么有些大团队虽然规模庞大，但却交付不出有价值的成果。而相比之下，小团队往往能高效交付，快速迭代。这些小团队不会把时间浪费在反复确认“能否交付？”、“需要多少工时？”、“去问问那个人需要几天？”这样的问题上，而是专注于开发，效率自然高得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to pull on that thread. I was thinking about the fact that you're building software for product teams and so you have a really unique perspective on product teams and you've seen a lot of product teams a lot more than a lot of other folks. And so I was curious what percentage of teams that you see are what you'd call like top notch, highly functional product teams?
turns.zh: 我想深入探讨一下这个问题。你为产品团队开发软件，因此对产品团队有着独特的见解，而且接触过的产品团队比大多数人都要多得多。我很好奇，你所接触的团队中，真正称得上顶尖、高效的产品团队比例是多少？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: That's a good question. I don't think I've got an answer there because it's going to be biased, because we naturally attract companies who self-select our way of working. We put on our site, no timelines come for the now, next, later. So it's going to be a much higher percentage. People don't sign up for demos with us if they know that they want a timeline nowadays, because we make it really clear. So I would say like 70% of them are like we want now, next, later. And I know that's not real. I know that's not the real state of people, of product teams out there.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。但我觉得我没法给出准确答案，因为这可能带有偏见——毕竟我们吸引的都是自觉认同我们工作方式的公司。我们在网站上明确标注“没有即时、下一步、稍后这些时间节点”。所以比例肯定会更高。如今，如果有人想了解即时的时间线，他们就不会来参加我们的演示，因为我们把规则说得很清楚。所以我估计70%的团队都希望“现在、下一步、稍后”这样的时间安排。而我知道这并不真实，这不是大多数产品团队的真实情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. So yeah, that makes sense.
turns.zh: 嗯，确实有道理。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: I do have a sense that it's increasing. So what I have found is years ago when we first started this thing off, no one was talking this way. It was a whole new concept and people are like, "No, this is crazy doc, you can't do it this way." Then over the years it has just become the natural way that people are working on it. People are going, "Of course this is the way that it works. Why would it work any other way?" It's becoming the expected way. Definitely changed the discourse and changed the expectations of the audience, I guess.
turns.zh: 我确实感觉这种趋势在增强。多年前我们刚开始做这件事时，没人会这样讨论。这是个全新的概念，人们会说：“不，博士，这太疯狂了，你不能这样做。”但多年来，这已经成了人们自然的工作方式。人们会说：“这当然是正确的做法。为什么还要用其他方式呢？” 它正在成为被期待的工作方式。这无疑改变了讨论的方向，也改变了观众的期望。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Putting the now next later piece to the site for one moment. I'm curious what else have you seen separates the best product teams from mediocre product teams? In terms of how they execute, the people they hire, processes, is there anything else that you've noticed of just like this team, when I think of teams that are functioning super well? Other than implementing this process you're recommending, is there anything else that often comes up?
turns.zh: 先把现在、接下来、稍后这套流程放到一边，暂且不谈。我很好奇，在优秀的产品团队和平庸的产品团队之间，还有哪些关键差异？从执行能力、团队组建、流程管理等方面，您是否注意到过类似的差距？当我想到那些运作极为高效的团队时，除了您提到的流程优化，还有什么其他关键要素？除了推行您所推荐的流程外，还有哪些常见的改进方向？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah, a couple things. A focus on discovery. So this ability to spend time in discovery and asking questions of customers and constantly being able to iterate based on that. And psychological safety, so teams who are able to question each other, speak up when they see that things are wrong, question what's going on at the senior level, question what's going on at different team levels, and generally just have the good sense of what's going on across their business because they're allowed to ask those questions, less silos.
turns.zh: 是的，有几个关键点：一是注重探索。即团队能投入充足的时间进行用户调研，不断迭代优化。二是心理安全感的营造。团队成员要敢于质疑彼此，及时指出问题所在，挑战高层决策，审视不同团队的运作模式。最重要的是，他们有权畅所欲言，获取全局视角——因为这种开放的沟通文化打破了信息壁垒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks. What's a lasting change that a team has made that made them significantly better at building product? Is it these two things, doing more discovery and maybe more safety? I imagine part of your answer will be implementing this way of working of now, next, later. Is there anything else that comes to mind? "Wow, wow, this one team did this one thing and it made things so much better for them."
turns.zh: 感谢您的分享。团队通过加强探索和提升安全感，能显著提升产品研发能力吗？您提到的“现在、接下来、稍后”流程是否是关键手段？是否还有其他案例能说明这种转变带来的显著提升？比如某个团队实施了某项举措后，业绩突飞猛进。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Like retrospectives. Retrospectives make such a big difference because they are indicative of psychological safety, which underpins so much, right? Once you start building in this psychological safety, the ability to ask questions and to start saying, "What are we doing that's working? What are we doing that's not working? Okay, determine that something doesn't work. Are we allowed to go change it? Okay, we are allowed to go change it." Okay, this is a team who's now changing their situation. They're talking to each other, they're learning from each other, and they're making a concerted effort to do so. And so these are the teams who are constantly learning, iterating, and moving forwards.
turns.zh: 比如定期复盘。复盘机制能有效提升心理安全感，而心理安全感是团队运作的基石。一旦团队建立起这种文化，成员就能主动反思：哪些方法有效？哪些环节需要改进？当发现问题时，他们敢于质疑现状，敢于挑战高层决策，敢于跨团队协作。这样的团队才能持续学习、迭代、前进。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And they naturally move towards things like now, next, later. They naturally move towards things like doing discovery, because these are just, I don't know, they're kind of common sense. They're not setting in stone expectations of what's going to be done and when. Because that was really only done because some head honcho wanted to see that information. That wasn't psychological safety. That was somebody pinning them down by the neck saying, "Tell me what's going to be done and when." Psychological safety is just saying, "Hey, tell me as much information as you know and then do discovery to learn as much as you can, so that we can move forward with this." It's all about just talking to your teammates and getting the most information as you can from the resources you have, making the most of the collective intelligence that you have within your company.
turns.zh: 而“现在、接下来、稍后”流程自然会水到渠成地出现。探索思维的养成同样重要，因为这本质上是常识。不再强制规定任务的时间表和执行标准，而是让团队成员充分收集信息、开展探索，最终形成共识。这才是真正的团队协作——通过与同事坦诚交流，充分利用现有资源和集体智慧，推动项目进展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to the now, next, later approach, you're often doing something really hard at companies, which is changing their way of working and changing their product culture. And I'm curious what you've learned about what it takes to change product development culture and product culture and the way of working at larger companies.
turns.zh: 回到“现在、接下来、稍后”流程，企业推行新流程往往面临巨大挑战，需要彻底改变产品开发文化和组织架构。我很好奇，在大型企业中，如何有效重塑产品开发文化和工作方式？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Larger companies are tough. They're tougher. I think of culture as calcification. So calcification being the limestone that is built up as watered run over and that sort of thing. And in order to fix it, you can kind of chip it off over time. You can't just fix it all in one go. And so in order to fix it, you've got to chip away at it. You've got to find a small pocket somewhere. You've got to make use of the tools that you've got. So sometimes it might be finding a small subset of the company and saying, 'Hey, here's the startup lab within the business. Let's let them run off and go do something." Because changing the mindset of the whole company is just too difficult. It's set in stone, and it's stuck where it is and can't change them all at once. But we can change this one little space right here, because we've got a shit hot leader who knows what they're doing and we can take this pocket of people and go do something here.
turns.zh: 大型公司确实很难管。它们更难管。我把文化比作钙化。钙化就像石灰岩，水流冲刷后会逐渐堆积起来。要想解决这个问题，只能一点点削弱它。不能一蹴而就。必须逐步推进，找到合适的突破口。利用现有资源，比如在公司内部成立创业实验室，让他们去尝试创新。毕竟改变整个公司的思维模式太难了。这种思维模式根深蒂固，一时半刻难以转变。但我们可以先在某个小范围里突破，因为我们有极具远见的领导者，他们知道该怎么做。只要能集结一批志同道合的人，就能有所作为。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And then they're going to teach the rest of the company. They're going to teach this section and then this section and then this section. You don't have to go and change the whole company all at once, but it does take buy-in from above. And sometimes that can be really difficult to take, because the incentives from above are often misaligned with the incentives that it takes to get a company moving this direction.
turns.zh: 然后他们会把新方法传授给其他部门，先教这个部门，再教那个部门。没必要一下子改变整个公司，但这需要高层的支持。有时候高层的激励机制和推动公司变革的方向不一致，这确实很难达成共识。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Ultimately, a lot of these larger companies, they're incentivized to keep the company as stable as possible, to keep the company just growing quarter on quarter. Which is great for the stock market, they love that stability, they love that quarter on quarter growth. But if the company is actually under threat from startups, if you're a big bank, you're in health tech, something like that, you almost certainly have startups nipping at your heels. And the reality is that you probably have enough cash to make it for the next 20 years or so, but over time it's going to get bitten away at.
turns.zh: 归根结底，很多大公司更倾向于保持现状，维持季度营收增长。这对股市来说不错，但现实是，初创公司正从各方面蚕食他们的市场份额。比如银行业、医疗科技等领域，初创公司都在紧追不舍。即便你手头有足够的现金维持未来20年运营，但时间一长，总会被一点点侵蚀。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And you've got smaller startups who are going to take the juicier, more interesting parts of your business and leave you with the tougher parts of your business. Take HSBC versus all the companies who are coming out with got a Starling account here and I've got a mortgage with somebody else and you've got your savings account somewhere else. You've got all these smaller startups nipping at their heels. These companies are going to nip away at these larger businesses and if these larger companies don't actually do something with it, they're actually going to end up losing this ability to innovate themselves. And so these companies are essentially stuck in this pattern where they want to continue growing and yet they're not going to, they're going to end up not being willing to take the dip to move upwards.
turns.zh: 小型初创公司会抢走你业务中更诱人、更有趣的部分，而把难题留给你。比如汇丰银行面对那些推出星星账户的公司，你的房贷在别家银行，储蓄账户又另寻他处。这类初创公司会不断蚕食大公司的市场份额。如果大公司不采取行动，最终将丧失自我创新的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the biggest company that you've implemented this new way of building? And is that how you approached it, you found a team within the larger company to roll out this new-
turns.zh: 你曾在哪家大公司实施过这种创新模式？是如何操作的——在大公司内部组建团队推行新模式吗？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... yeah, this framework?
turns.zh: ……是的，就是这个框架？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah. So that's how it generally works with the way that we work with our enterprise rollouts is like we worked with large enterprises of governments as well. It generally starts with an advocate, somebody who gets the way that we're working, a division, a department, and then it starts from there. Sometimes what we'll find is that we'll get one or two, sometimes three or four many groups starting and then they'll start banding together and saying, "Hey, no, we're starting a thing here." Once that starts happening, it's easier to start that conversation saying, "Okay, yeah, we've got a whole thing going here. Let's talk to the person who is the VP of strategy, or who owns the tech area," and then we can have a bigger conversation.
turns.zh: 是的。这就是我们在企业推广中通常的做法，比如我们也与政府大型企业合作。通常会从一个倡导者开始，他要让别人理解我们的工作方式，可能是一个部门或分支机构，然后从那里逐步展开。有时我们会发现，一开始会有一两个甚至三四个团队开始行动，随后他们会逐渐联合起来，说：“嘿，不行，我们要在这里开展一项工作。” 一旦这种情况出现，就更容易开启对话，比如：“好的，我们这边已经全面开展了，让我们和战略副总裁或者技术部门负责人聊聊。” 这样就能进行更深入的沟通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the impact that you saw at that company having taken on this new way of building product?
turns.zh: 在那家公司采用这种新产品开发方式后，你观察到有什么影响吗？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So we're in the middle of a key tool in the middle of transformations right now, which is fascinating to see. These are multi-year pieces of work where you're seeing it being used for ongoing products that are being used and delivered as we speak, as well as part of a mindset shift within the business. Because one of the things about ProdPad is that it's not just a tool to help you deliver your products, it's actually a tool that helps you become a better product manager. It sets in stone better product management practices. Once you start using it, it makes it difficult to go back to bad product management practices.
turns.zh: 目前我们正处于变革进程中的一个关键工具阶段，看到这一切真是令人兴奋。这些都是多年的工作成果，你会看到它被用于正在开发的产品，这些产品在我们交谈时就已经在应用了，同时它也推动了企业内部思维模式的转变。因为ProdPad不仅仅是一个帮助你交付产品的工具，它实际上还能帮助你成为更优秀的产品经理。它将更好的产品管理实践固定下来，只要你开始使用它，就很难再回到糟糕的产品管理模式中去。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: When you create a roadmap in ProdPad, it makes difficult to add features and dates to the roadmap. It makes it difficult to make a timeline based roadmap. It makes it difficult to add ideas to the backlog that are not thought through, because it asks questions, thoughtful questions, like what problem does this solve? And why would you want to solve it? And what are the outcomes? And what did you get?So it makes it difficult to fall into a build trap with just saying, "Here's stuff to build," and we built it, and move on to the next thing, like a lot of dev tools are designed to do. Because it has spaces in there to say, "Did you measure success? And was it successful or not successful? This roadmap thing is completed, what was the outcome of it?" So by creating all these spaces, it creates all these reminders for the team to go back and think about this stuff before they do work and after they do work. So it actually actively helps them become better product teams and more cognizant of this sort of work.
turns.zh: 在ProdPad中创建路线图时，很难在路线图中添加功能和日期，也很难基于时间线创建路线图。更难的是将未经深思熟虑的想法添加到待办事项列表中，因为它会提出深思熟虑的问题，比如：这个问题解决了什么需求？你为什么要解决这个问题？结果是什么？你得到了什么？因此，这很难让人陷入只说“有东西要建了”然后就开始建造的陷阱，就像许多开发工具设计的那样。因为ProdPad中有专门的空间让你回答：“你衡量过成功吗？成功了吗？不成功吗？路线图完成了，结果如何？” 通过创建这些空间，它不断提醒团队在开始工作前和结束工作后回过头来思考这些问题。因此，它实际上积极帮助他们成为更优秀的产品团队，更清楚地认识到这项工作的重要性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If someone wanted to experiment with now, next, later, what would be a good place to go and just start to play around with it?
turns.zh: 如果有人现在想尝试“现在、下一步、稍后”模式，哪里是开始尝试的好地方？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: I mean, you can start a free trial in ProdPad, you can start playing around with it. We even have a sandbox mode. You just go to sandbox.prodpad.com where it's got example versions of roadmaps, best practice roadmaps that you can just start playing with. You don't even need a login or a credit card. It's got OKRs and roadmaps and ideas and experiments, feedback. You see how it all sort of fits together. But honestly, a now, next, later roadmap can be done with Post-It Notes on the wall. It's just about saying, "What problems do you have? Let's lay them out in order and just check them with other people."
turns.zh: 我的意思是，你可以在ProdPad上开始免费试用，随便玩一玩。我们甚至还有沙盒模式。你只需访问sandbox.prodpad.com，那里有示例路线图、最佳实践路线图，你可以随意尝试。甚至不需要登录或信用卡。它涵盖OKR、路线图、想法、实验、反馈等功能。你可以看到它们如何完美融合。但说实话，创建“现在、下一步、稍后”路线图也可以用墙上的便利贴来完成。关键在于说：“你有什么问题？让我们按顺序列出来，然后和其他人一起核对。”

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So the whole point about a roadmap is that it's not designed to be your plan. I think about it as being a prototype for your strategy. What I mean by that is we talk about prototyping all the time in the lean world and a prototype is essentially a way of checking your assumptions. Generally, we think about it in terms of a design or like a model, but think about it at the strategy level. So at the feature level, you'd prototype by doing a design, a mockup, and you take that mockup and you'd share it with somebody, and say, "Here's a mockup of the feature that I'm trying to build. What do you think?" And they tell you what's right or wrong, and you'd add some new copy or a button to make it more clear, and you throw out the original prototype, because it wasn't very good and you make a new one.
turns.zh: 因此，路线图的核心意义在于，它并非旨在成为你的最终计划。在我看来，它更像是你的战略规划的原型。我的意思是，在精益管理领域，我们经常谈论原型设计，而原型本质上就是验证假设的一种方式。通常，我们会从设计或模型层面来理解它，但在战略层面同样适用。在功能层面，你可以通过设计原型、制作模型来进行原型验证。然后，你将模型分享给别人，问他们：“这是我要开发的功能，你觉得怎么样？”对方会指出优缺点，你会添加新的文案或按钮来优化，最终舍弃旧的原型，因为它不够完善，再重新制作新版本。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So the value isn't the prototype, the value is in the prototyping process. The value isn't in your roadmap, The value is in the roadmapping process. What you're actually doing is laying out your assumptions of the problems that you're solving. So you're saying, "I think we have this problem then this problem. What do you think?" The whole point is that you just share your early assumptions with other people on the team, with customers, even, like anybody, who will listen. And just check that you're on the right path. And if they say, "Oh, actually I thought that it was going to go this way, this way, then this way, or that way, then the other way, and what about this problem?" You've actually learned something. You can adjust your prototype for your strategy, you can adjust your roadmap there and your roadmap all of a sudden becomes stronger, becomes better there.
turns.zh: 原型的价值并不在于其本身，而在于原型设计的过程。路线图的价值也不在于最终成果，而在于制定路线图的过程。实际上，你是在列出自己对所要解决问题的假设清单。你会说：“我认为我们面临这个问题，然后是那个问题。你们怎么看？”关键在于，你要与团队成员、客户甚至任何愿意倾听的人分享早期的假设，验证自己的思路是否正确。如果对方说：“哦，实际上我认为事情会这样发展、那样发展，或者反过来发展，还有这个问题呢？” 那你就学到了东西。你可以调整战略原型，优化路线图，这样你的路线图会变得更强大、更完善。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For folks that are listening and they're just like, "Nah, this is never going to work where I work. It's just too out there, too radical. No deadlines, that's crazy." I know you're not saying no deadlines, but less deadlines. What are the most powerful three bullet points you could share with listeners that are just like, :Here's why you should have confidence this might actually work at your company."
turns.zh: 对于那些听众可能会说：“不行，在我公司这永远行不通。太激进了，太不现实了。没有截止日期？简直疯了。” 我知道你不是说完全没有截止日期，而是说减少截止日期。能否给听众分享三个最有力的要点，帮助他们理解为何相信这种方法在自己的公司也能奏效？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Other teams are already working this way. Product people are the only ones who seem to be pinned down to be required to give concrete dates as to when things are going to be delivered in this way. Your sales team isn't asked to give exact delivery dates on their work. They work in a very experimentation led way as well. You are VP sales or VP revenue or whoever doesn't go to a board meeting and say, "We're going to close the Acme deal at the end of October for a million pounds." They don't know that. What they do know is that they have a process by which they're going to fill a pipeline, and almost certainly they're going to be able to close a million pounds or a million dollars worth of sales, but they can't tell you who it's going to come from or how that's going to work.
turns.zh: 其他团队已经在这样工作了。只有产品团队似乎被要求必须给出确切的交付日期。销售团队则无需为他们的工作设定精确的交付期限。他们同样以实验为主导的方式工作。比如，销售副总裁或营收副总裁等职位的人不会在董事会会议上说：“我们将在10月底完成与Acme公司的100万英镑交易。” 他们不知道具体日期，但他们知道有一个流程来填充销售漏斗，几乎可以确定能达成100万英镑或美元的销售目标，但他们无法预测具体客户或成交方式。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: What they're going to say is, "Give me a quarter million dollars worth of investment into my team, which I'm going to spend that on my account executives, my sales team. They're going to pick up the phone and do a bunch of calls." Think of these calls as experiments. These calls, some of them are going to work, some of them are going to fail. They don't know which ones are going to work and which ones are going to fail. What they do know is that by using a script and by picking up the phone and calling people, some are going to work. And by the end of the quarter someone's going to buy. And they know this because last quarter someone bought and the quarter before that someone bought, they just don't know who's going to buy. If they did know who's going to buy, then they would just call those people and not everybody else.
turns.zh: 他们要说的是：“给我25万美元投资我的团队，我会把这笔钱花在客户经理和销售团队上。他们会拿起电话打一堆电话。” 把这些电话视为实验。有些电话会成功，有些会失败。他们不知道哪些会成功，哪些会失败。但他们知道，通过使用脚本和主动打电话，总会有一些电话取得成效。到季度末，总会有人下单。这是因为上季度有人下单了，前季度也有人下单，他们只是不知道具体是谁会下单。如果他们知道是谁会下单，就只会给这些人打电话，而不是其他人。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Same thing. You're not asking for any more leeway than your sales team. You're saying that you want a quarter million dollars worth of investment, and you're going to spend it on your team who's going to run experiments, right? It's going to be trying this change on the interface or that tweak to the pricing or that change to the positioning or whatever you're going to do. Some of these experiments are going to fail and some are going to succeed. You don't know which ones. But that's okay, you know that by the end of the quarter, enough are going to succeed that you're probably going to move the right numbers in the right direction.
turns.zh: 道理是一样的。你要求的灵活度并不比销售团队多。你说你需要25万美元的投资，然后把钱花在团队上，让他们去尝试各种改变——比如调整界面、调整定价、调整定位策略等等。有些尝试会失败，有些会成功。你不知道哪些会成功，但没关系。你知道到季度末，总会有足够多的尝试成功，这样你们就能朝着正确的方向推进关键数据了。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: So you're not asking for any more leeway than your salesperson. What you should be able to do is point at how many experiments you ran the previous quarter, and what numbers moved in the right direction. You should be accountable for your experiments and how you're spending the money and what you're doing. But you shouldn't be accountable for saying what is going to work before you know what's going to work yet. And that's the problem with this timeline delivery, Magic 8 Ball that we're asked to give.
turns.zh: 所以你要求的灵活度并不比销售人员多。你们应该能够列出上季度进行了多少次实验，以及哪些数据朝着正确的方向发展了。你应该为自己的实验、资金使用和行动负责。但你不应该在还不确定结果的情况下就承诺什么会成功。这就是我们被要求提供的这种时间线交付和魔术8球式的预测存在的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. Two last questions before we get to a very exciting lightning round, which I didn't tell you about. We'll see how that goes. So one is you have an interesting framework for coming up with a product vision, and I don't know if you have this in your head loaded up, but I'm curious how you think about coming up with a product vision. You have this really handy little framework, and vision is always this thing that people are like, "Man, how do I come up with a vision? How do I phrase a vision? How do I even visualize my team's mission?" Can you share that with us, if you have that in your head?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个问题。再提两个问题，然后我们就进入一个非常精彩的闪电问答环节，我之前没跟你们提过。我们看看效果如何。第一个问题是，你有一个制定产品愿景的有趣框架，我不知道你们有没有记在心里，但我很好奇你是如何思考产品愿景的。你有一个非常方便的小框架，而愿景总是让人们头疼的问题：“天哪，我该怎么制定愿景？怎么用语言表达愿景？甚至怎么让团队理解我们的使命？” 如果你记得的话，能跟我们分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: The product vision template, you might actually recognize it from the Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm book. It's the elevator pitch template. But I like it because it answers the same sort of questions that you need to answer for a product vision template. So it asks things like, for your target customer, who the statement of need or the opportunity. The product name is a product category. What's the reason to buy? And then say, unlike this alternative our product, and then say what this statement of differentiation is. So it's actually a template that we have available on our site, and you can actually fill out as part of our product canvas in ProdPad. So happy to share that link with you, so you can link it up and send it to your audience here, Lenny.
turns.zh: 产品愿景模板，你们可能从杰弗里·摩尔的《跨越鸿沟》一书中认识它。这是电梯游说模板。但我喜欢它，因为它回答了制定产品愿景模板时需要回答的相同问题。比如，针对目标客户，需求或机会是什么。产品名称是产品类别。购买理由是什么？然后说与竞争对手相比，我们产品的差异点是什么。所以这实际上是一个模板，我们在网站上提供，你们可以在ProdPad的产品画布中填写。很乐意把链接分享给你们，这样你们就可以把链接发给这里的听众了，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Yeah, we'll put that in the show notes. I think that's the same framework as the positioning exercise. I might be wrong, but if so, that's cool. So basically you could use your positioning work to help figure out your vision. And just like a vision, it's basically a vision statement, it's not necessarily the vision for your product, it's just kind of how you think about where it's going to go.
turns.zh: 太棒了。是的，我们会把这部分内容放进节目笔记里。我觉得这和定位练习的框架是一样的。我可能记错了，但即便如此也没关系。所以基本上，你可以利用你的定位工作来帮助你明确自己的愿景。和愿景一样，定位陈述不一定是针对产品的，它只是你对产品发展方向的思考。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. The last question, you were a PM now you're founder, so you moved from PM to founder, and a lot of PMs, imagine being founders someday. I'm curious if you have any advice for folks that are currently PMs that may want to be founders in the future. What do you think they should be working on, focusing on, skills, vision rebuilding, things they should be doing to help them in that future career?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。最后一个问题，你现在是产品经理，现在又成了创始人，所以你从产品经理转型成了创始人。很多产品经理都想象着自己未来能成为创始人。我很好奇，你对那些目前是产品经理、未来可能想成为创始人的人有什么建议吗？你觉得他们应该专注于哪些方面？技能提升、愿景重建，还是做些其他事情来为未来的职业生涯做好准备？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Being a PM actually provides you with a lot of the skills and background to be a founder, to be a CEO. It gives you a lot of chance to work with a lot of the different teams and see a lot of the underpinnings of how business works. I was really lucky in previous roles where I got to work very closely with leadership in a few different roles before I took the step up to take on my own thing. So I felt as if I'd seen it in a few different ways, done well and done badly, and so I got a chance to sort of say, "Ah, I think I could do this. Yeah, go on."
turns.zh: 实际上成为产品经理能为你成为创始人或CEO奠定很多基础。它给了你很多机会与不同团队合作，了解商业运作的底层逻辑。我很幸运，在之前的职位中，我有机会与多个部门的领导密切合作，然后才接手自己的项目。因此，我觉得自己从不同角度观察过这个行业，既有成功的经验，也有失败的教训，这让我有信心说“嗯，我觉得我能做到。没错，继续吧。”

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: One of the things that struck me is it's not as hard as it looks, and it's also harder than it looks. There's things that you get started and you go, oh, no one's going to stop you from doing this. You've got lots of leeway. You can just do it, and you've got lots of freedom to run your business how you want to do it. There's lots of resource out there. As long as you surround yourself with people, you're always going to be able to find people to advise you and to help you along the way. And there's always going to be bumps. You don't know what they're going to be yet. There's always going to be things that are going to come by and side swipe you, but that's always the case that you had when you are product manager as well.
turns.zh: 让我印象深刻的是，这份工作比看起来容易，也比看起来难得多。有些事情刚开始时你会想，哦，没人会阻止你做这件事。你有很多自由发挥的空间，可以随心所欲地经营自己的事业。市场上有很多资源，只要你身边有合适的人，总能找到愿意指导和帮助你的人。但难免会遇到挫折。你现在还不知道这些挫折是什么，总会有突如其来的问题把你击倒，但这也是你担任产品经理时常遇到的情况。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: And just be ready for those and be ready to take it on the chin and deal with them as they come. Best thing you can do is surround yourself with people so that you've got somebody to go to for each thing. Going, "Oh, when I run into a problem that has to do with this, I can talk to this person. When I run into a problem that has to do with this, I talked to one of these people." And figure it out as you go. Take each thing a day at time. Certainly, don't stop yourself from starting a business or starting your own thing, just because you don't think that you know how to do it yet. You will figure it out as you go ahead. People less capable than you have figured it out.
turns.zh: 要做好准备迎接这些挑战，坦然面对它们。最重要的是，要确保身边有能解答各种问题的人。“遇到与这个相关的难题，可以找这个人聊聊。遇到那个问题，可以找那个人咨询。”这样就能边做边学。每天专注于当下的问题。当然，不要因为觉得自己还不知道怎么做就放弃创业或自主创业。边做边学，总能找到解决办法。比你能力弱的人都成功过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. We've reached our lightning round. The way it's going to work, I'm going to ask you five questions real quick. Whatever comes to mind, share an answer.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们要进入闪电问答环节了。接下来我会快速问你五个问题。想到什么就回答什么。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If nothing comes to mind, that's also cool. Sound good?
turns.zh: 如果暂时想不到答案，也没关系。听起来不错吧？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.zh: 《盈利的艺术》，我觉得这本书非常棒。

turns.en: Sandman is-

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: ……一部英国剧集，对吧？

turns.zh: 哦，它是英国的。没错，是尼尔·盖曼创作的。是的，非常棒。但绝对不适合儿童观看。我原以为可能适合，肯定不适合。

turns.en: Noted. What's another favorite podcast of yours other than the one you're currently on?
turns.zh: 明白了。除了你现在参与的那个播客，还有你喜欢的其他播客吗？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Ooh, Startups For the Rest Of Us.
turns.zh: 哦，《为我们其他人打造的初创公司》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I haven't heard of that one. Tell us more.
turns.zh: 哇，我没听说过这个。多讲讲。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Basically, it's Rob Walling's podcast and it's for startups that are either bootstrapped or alt funded. Basically, the startups that aren't the one percent top end funded, unicorns, but the startups for the rest of us.
turns.zh: 基本上，这是罗伯·沃林的播客，专为自力更生或另类融资的初创公司打造的。也就是那些不是顶级融资、独角兽级别的初创公司，而是面向普通人的初创公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What's a favorite interview question of yours that you like to ask?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: I like asking people what problems that they're looking to solve. Why are they coming to this table?
turns.zh: 我喜欢问人们他们想要解决什么问题。他们为什么来参加这次会议？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very PMy question.
turns.zh: 很典型的 PME 问题。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Who else in the industry do you most respect as a thought leader? Who comes to mind?
turns.zh: 业内还有哪位思想领袖最令你尊敬？你能想到谁？

turns.en: I've got to give a shout out to Christina Wodtke. I had a great conversation with her yesterday, and I've had a chance to chat with her a number of times over the years, but she's just got this illustrious career. She's been part of so many amazing teams, built some amazing things, written some amazing books, and is also just an all round amazing product person and amazing person all in one.
turns.zh: 我得特别提一下克里斯蒂娜·沃德克。我昨天和她进行了很棒的对话，多年来我也多次与她交流，但她的职业生涯堪称辉煌。她曾参与许多出色的团队，打造了不少优秀成果，写过几本很棒的书，而且她本身就是一位全能的产品达人。

turns.en: Janna, this has been amazing. I think we covered a lot of different topics, more than we often cover in a podcast like this. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they'd like to reach out and learn more? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 詹娜，这次访谈太棒了。我觉得我们探讨了许多不同的话题，比我们在这种播客中通常讨论的要多得多。最后两个问题，如果听众想了解更多信息，如何能找到你？以及听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Wonderful. Hi, I'm Janna Bastow. You can find me all on Twitter, I'm simplybastow there. Or come find me on LinkedIn, connect with me, I'm Janna Bastow. I'm easy to find there. And come check out ProdPad. It'd be wonderful to get your feedback on it, because we are a team of product people and we love hearing what other product people think of the product. We're always open to feedback. We're constantly pushing new releases. So check it out, try the sandbox. We'd love to hear from you.
turns.zh: 太好了。你好，我是詹娜·巴斯托。你们可以在 Twitter 上找到我，账号是 simplybastow。或者来 LinkedIn 找我，联系我，我是詹娜·巴斯托。在那里很容易找到我。还有来试试 ProdPad。我们很乐意听取你们的反馈，因为我们是一个产品团队，我们喜欢听其他产品人对产品的看法。我们随时开放反馈，不断推出新版本。所以来试试吧，在沙盒中玩玩。我们期待听到你们的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Thank you for being here, Janna.
turns.zh: 太棒了。谢谢你参加访谈，詹娜。

turns.speaker: Janna Bastow
turns.en: Of course, thanks so much.
turns.zh: 当然，非常感谢。
